metadata.description: Human dual-process performance benchmarks from published cognitive psychology studies
metadata.note: S2-S1 gaps reflect within-study contrasts: System 1 = intuitive/fast/unreflective response; System 2 = deliberate/slow/reflective response. Absolute accuracy values are not directly comparable to LLM scores; the intended use is pattern comparison of gap magnitudes across task categories.

crt_classic.source: Frederick, S. (2005). Cognitive reflection and decision making. Journal of Economic Perspectives, 19(4), 25-42.
crt_classic.notes: System 1 = initial intuitive response rate correct; System 2 = accuracy after deliberate reflection. MIT students scored 48% on initial intuitive attempt. Large gap reflects that CRT items are specifically designed to elicit an incorrect intuitive response.

base_rate_neglect.source: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1973). On the psychology of prediction. Psychological Review, 80(4), 237-251.
base_rate_neglect.notes: System 1 = ignoring base rates, relying on representativeness heuristic; System 2 = accuracy after explicit instruction to consider base rate information. Gap reflects difficulty of overriding intuitive representativeness reasoning.

syllogistic_reasoning.source: Evans, J. St. B. T., Barston, J. L., & Pollard, P. (1983). On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning. Memory & Cognition, 11(3), 295-306.
syllogistic_reasoning.notes: System 1 = belief-based responding on belief-inconsistent syllogisms; System 2 = logic-based responding after instruction to ignore prior beliefs. Gap reflects the belief-bias effect in deductive reasoning.

arithmetic_word_problems.source: Ashcraft, M. H. (1992). Cognitive arithmetic: A review of data and theory. Cognition, 44(1-2), 75-106.
arithmetic_word_problems.notes: System 1 = performance under time pressure (forced fast response); System 2 = unlimited time condition. Multi-step word problems. Gap reflects benefit of deliberate computation over rapid estimation.

simple_pattern_recognition.source: Stanovich, K. E., & West, R. F. (2000). Individual differences in reasoning: Implications for the rationality debate? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 23(5), 645-665.
simple_pattern_recognition.notes: System 1 = immediate response with no deliberation; System 2 = accuracy after reflection on easy pattern tasks. Minimal S2 advantage reflects ceiling-level intuitive performance on simple recognition tasks.

semantic_association.source: Thompson, V. A., Prowse Turner, J. A., & Pennycook, G. (2011). Intuition, reason and metacognition. Cognitive Psychology, 63(3), 107-140.
semantic_association.notes: System 1 = initial response associated with high feeling-of-rightness rating; System 2 = accuracy after reconsideration prompted by low initial confidence. Minimal gap for associative/semantic tasks consistent with automatic processing efficiency.

framing_effects.source: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1981). The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice. Science, 211(4481), 453-458.
framing_effects.notes: System 1 = susceptibility to framing (72% chose incorrectly in loss-frame condition despite identical expected value); System 2 = partial resistance after deliberation (45% susceptibility). Accuracy computed as proportion making frame-invariant choice. Gap reflects partial but incomplete override of framing by deliberate reasoning.

conjunction_fallacy.source: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1983). Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: The conjunction fallacy in probability judgment. Psychological Review, 90(4), 293-315.
conjunction_fallacy.notes: System 1 = Linda problem: 85% commit the conjunction fallacy (intuitive representativeness dominates); System 2 = accuracy after statistical training reduces fallacy rate to ~36%. Very large gap reflects how strongly intuitive representativeness reasoning overrides logical probability judgment.
